title: Kaddish is praise
hook: an Aramaic prayer praising God, said by mourners, that never mentions death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aleinu, the bow near the end of the service. Your line was bow now, and hope later. Today, a prayer people think they know.

In films and novels, the Kaddish usually turns up in one scene: the graveside, a son or daughter standing, a few murmured Aramaic words. It gets called the Jewish prayer for the dead. And mourners do say it. But read the words of the mourner's version, and something strange happens. There is no death in it. No grave, no loss, no person who has died, no afterlife. It doesn't even mention the mourner. It praises God, line after line, and closes by asking for peace.
screen: `THE PRAYER FOR THE DEAD?` → `NO DEATH IN IT.` → `PRAISE, THEN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Kaddish means holy, or sanctification. It's in Aramaic, the everyday language many Jews spoke in the time of the Talmud, not Hebrew. Its first words are yitgadal v'yitkadash shmeh rabba: magnified and sanctified be His great name. Those two verbs echo Ezekiel, in the old Jewish translation: "Thus will I magnify Myself, and sanctify Myself." Then it asks that God's kingship be established in our lives and our days, soon. At the center comes the line the whole congregation answers aloud: y'hei shmeh rabba, may His great name be blessed forever and ever. The Talmud treats that answer as huge. In tractate Shabbat, a teacher says whoever answers it with all their strength has a harsh decree against them torn up. Kaddish likely began not in mourning but in the study house: after a teacher finished a lesson, everyone praised God together. That version is still said after learning. In the service it comes in several forms. A short one marks the joints between sections, like a bookmark. A full one closes the main prayer. One follows study. And one is said by mourners. So when a mourner stands up, they aren't saying a prayer about death. They're leading the room in praise, at the very moment praise is hardest. Tomorrow, why they do it.
screen: `KADDISH: HOLY, IN ARAMAIC.` · `MAGNIFIED AND SANCTIFIED.` · `THE ROOM ANSWERS: MAY HIS NAME BE BLESSED.` · `FROM THE STUDY HOUSE.` · then, large: `NO DEATH IN IT.`

segments.voice: Bring back a word of praise you heard lately, a friend saying the sunset was beautiful, a child proud of a drawing, a grandparent thanking God for a meal, and hear it again. Then answer it quietly, amen, yes, so be it, because in the Kaddish the answering is half the prayer.
Kaddish. Holy, sanctification. An Aramaic prayer of pure praise, said by mourners and answered by everyone.
Your line: magnified and sanctified. The mourner leads, and the room answers. Day six hundred three, done.

howItsDone: Kaddish is said only with a minyan: the leader or the mourners recite it, and the congregation answers amen and the line y'hei shmeh rabba aloud. Different forms of it mark the sections of the service, close the Amidah, follow study, and are said by mourners.

chat.says: Isn't the Kaddish the Jewish prayer for the dead? What does it say about them?
options: Nothing, actually; it praises God and asks for peace, and mourners lead it.
It's a Hebrew lament for the one who died, said only beside the grave.
It describes the afterlife, so mourners know where their loved one went.
chat.meaning: The Mourner's Kaddish has no death in it: it's Aramaic praise, magnified and sanctified be His great name, closing with a request for peace.

Origin of the Kaddish in the study house (Kaddish d'Rabbanan) is a widely held scholarly view; phrased as 'likely'.

Forms listed: half Kaddish, full Kaddish (Titkabal), Kaddish d'Rabbanan, Mourner's Kaddish. The burial Kaddish (Kaddish d'Itchadata) does mention the revival of the dead; the claim 'no death in it' refers to the Mourner's Kaddish and the service forms. Keeper may want this nuance.
